title: House Robber II
statement:
This time the houses stand in a circle: the first house is a neighbour of the last one as well as the second. You still must not rob two neighbouring houses. Given `nums` with the money in each house in order around the circle, return the largest total you can rob.

With a single house there is nobody next to it, so you can rob it.

Constraints: 1 <= len(nums) <= 400; 0 <= nums[i] <= 400.

examples.explanation: The first and last houses are neighbours, so you can't take both 4s. Take 4 + 2 instead.
With three houses in a circle every pair is adjacent, so you can only rob one.
A lone house has no neighbours.

hints: Compare with the street version. Which pair of houses is newly adjacent here?
In any valid plan, can the first and the last house both be robbed? What does that tell you about the possible plans?
Try [5, 2, 6] and [2, 7, 9, 3, 1]. What goes wrong if you run the straight-street solution on the whole list?
Split the problem into two cases so that the first and last houses are never both available. Which houses does each case cover?
Run the straight-street solution twice, once without the last house and once without the first, and take the larger. Watch out for the single-house case.
followUps: What are the time and space complexity, and how many passes does your solution make over the input?
Why is it enough to consider two cases (skip the first house, or skip the last), even though a plan may skip both?
How do you avoid copying the list when you handle the two cases?
What would you do if the houses formed a binary tree instead of a street or a circle?
How would you report which houses to rob, not only the total?
idealAnswerPoints: Recognises the circle means the first and last houses can't both be robbed
Reduces the problem to two straight-street problems: houses 0..n-2 and houses 1..n-1
Reuses the take-or-skip DP from the linear version as a helper
Handles a single house separately so the two ranges don't both come out empty
States O(n) time and O(1) space
weakAnswerSigns: Runs the linear solution on the whole list and ignores the wrap-around
Excludes only the first house, or only the last, never trying both
Returns 0 for a single house because both sub-ranges are empty
Copies the list twice with slicing and doesn't mention the extra memory

rubric.correctness: Maximum total on every test, including one house, two houses, and lists where the best plan uses the first or the last house.
rubric.efficiency: Two linear passes, O(n) time. Anything exponential fails the 400-house inputs.
rubric.code_quality: One reusable helper for the straight-street case; the single-house edge case handled explicitly.
rubric.communication: Explains the two-case split before coding and shows with a small example why the full-list answer would be wrong.
